sections.html:
Bristol in Bucks County is most often Bristol Township, the large municipality of about 54,000 residents that includes Levittown neighborhoods, Croydon and Bath. A sale there runs through the agreement of sale, a township change of occupancy approval on resale, settlement and a deed recorded with the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. Bristol Borough is a separate municipality with its own rules, so check which one your address falls in. Your tax bill names the municipality and school district, and the Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals can tell you where the parcel sits.

The township's Building and Planning Department is at 2501 Bath Road and answers questions at 215-785-3680. Call before you list, so you know what the office will want to see for a resale in your part of the township.

Buyers here are mostly owners. Owner-occupied homes make up 72.4 percent of housing units for 2020 to 2024. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $315,500, median gross rent is $1,245, and the 20,908 households have a median income of $79,101. Population was 54,291 in the 2020 census and an estimated 54,063 in July 2025. Only 92.2 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so houses do not turn over often and a well-kept one stands out. Commutes average 27.4 minutes, and the township sits at the junction of Interstate 95, the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Interstate 295.

The wettest day since 1981 delivered 6.42 inches of rain on August 27, 2011, so check basements and sump pumps before showings.

The Resolution 2026-25 fee schedule sets a $100 charge for a residential change of occupancy on resale, and a second inspection costs $40 if one is needed. Fees most sellers run into are below.

FeeAmount
Residential resale change of occupancy$100
Second inspection, if needed$40
Four-year tax certification$35 ($50 rush)
Sewer certification$50
Lien fee$180
Residential sewer charge$111.03 per quarter
Refuse user fee$400 a year, billed on the tax bill

Order the tax and sewer certifications before settlement is scheduled, so they are back when the title company asks.

The township's fee schedule lists a real estate transfer tax of 1 percent of the purchase price, split 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the Bristol Township School District. Add the state's 1 percent and the total on a sale is 2 percent. Grantor and grantee are jointly liable under state law, so the agreement of sale should say who pays.

Township millage for 2026 lists these funds: general 16.58 mills, debt 2.45, capital improvement 1.5, fire protection 3, recreation 0.9 and rescue squad 0.55. That adds to 24.98 mills before the school and county rates.

A buyer must send contact information to the Bucks County Board of Assessment within 30 days of buying, under Act 29. Tell your buyer at closing, because the notice is theirs to send and it is easy to forget in the rush after settlement.

Annual appeals are due each August, with a $75 filing fee per parcel, and any change from an annual appeal takes effect the following tax year. Appeals are filed by the aggrieved party of record. Call the board for the current year's date.

sections.h2: How the township permit process runs
sections.html:
The township's permit page describes six steps from application to a Certificate of Approval, and a finished project closes the file for the next owner. Applications go through the township's online self-service portal or at the municipal building.

  • Submit the application, and staff check that forms and fees are complete.
  • Township professionals review the plans against state and local construction codes and zoning.
  • The application is approved or denied; a denial can be corrected or taken to the appeals board.
  • Once the permit is paid for and issued, it must be posted where the public can see it, and approved plans stay on site.
  • Inspections happen in two phases, rough and final, and you call 48 hours ahead to schedule each one.
  • A Certificate of Approval issues when all work complies.

If an inspector finds unapproved work, the township demands compliance, and a stop work order follows when compliance is not found. Sellers with open permits should finish the final inspection before listing.

Unpermitted work is the common obstacle, because the township doubles permit fees when it finds work done without a permit and may add court fines. Permits are needed for additions, fences, renovations, decks, pools, demolitions and electrical, plumbing and HVAC equipment.

All contractors working in the township must be registered, and registrations are renewed annually from January through December. The township also asks everyone who lives or works there to complete a municipal and school income tax registration through Keystone Collection. Before you list, confirm that finals were signed off on past projects.

sections.h2: Order of steps for a Bristol Township sale
sections.html:
1. Confirm the house is in the township, not the borough, using your tax bill.
  2. Order the four-year tax certification and the sewer certification early. A rush on the tax certification costs more.
  3. Call the Building and Planning Department about the $100 change of occupancy approval and book the inspection.
  4. Fix anything flagged. If a second inspection is needed it is $40.
  5. Clear any open permit with a final inspection, since the township asks for 48 hours of notice to schedule each one.
  6. Pay any lien or sewer balance, then settle and record the deed with the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds.

Doing the certifications first usually keeps the closing on the date you agreed.

The fee schedule lists an annual rental fee of $100 for a single-family dwelling and an occupied rental fine of $320. A landlord selling a tenant-occupied house should check the rental status first and gather any records the buyer will want. Read the lease for notice terms before you schedule showings or the resale inspection.

sections.h2: Ways to sell fast in Bristol Township
sections.html: You can list with an agent, sell on your own or accept a cash offer. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the change of occupancy approval and the tax and sewer certifications still apply. Ask for any offer in writing and compare them by the check you receive after fees, taxes and any repairs.

faqs.q: Do I need a use and occupancy inspection to sell a house in Bristol Township?
faqs.a: The township's 2026 fee schedule lists a $100 residential change of occupancy charge on resale and $40 for a second inspection if one is needed. Call 215-785-3680 to confirm the steps for your address.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on a Bristol Township sale?
faqs.a: The contract sets who pays, but state law makes seller and buyer jointly liable. The total is 2 percent: 1 percent to Pennsylvania, 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the school district.

faqs.q: What certifications does the township issue at sale?
faqs.a: Tax and sewer certifications. A four-year tax certification costs $35, or $50 rushed, and a sewer certification costs $50. Order them before settlement is scheduled.

faqs.q: Is Bristol Township the same as Bristol Borough?
faqs.a: No. They are separate municipalities in Bucks County with separate rules and officials. The figures on this page describe the township.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Bristol Township assessment after selling?
faqs.a: Appeals are filed by the aggrieved party of record. Annual appeals are due each August, and changes take effect the following tax year, so call the Bucks County board for the current date.
